claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of pvf1 in adult male flies leads to increased lipid droplet size in adipose tissue cells.
source: Strikingly, knockdown of pvf1 in the adult muscle (musts>pvf1-i), but not in other organs such as the gut, adipose tissue, or oenocytes, was associated with a severe obesity phenotype characterized by increased lipid droplet size in the adipose tissue cells (Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and imaging showing increased lipid droplet size, as presented in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of pvf1 leads to increased accumulation of lipid droplets in oenocytes.
source: Additionally, the experimental animals showed increased accumulation of lipid droplets in the oenocytes which are normally devoid of or have very few lipid droplets (Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining showing lipid accumulation in oenocytes, as presented in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of pvf1 significantly increases whole animal triacylglycerol (TAG) content compared to control flies.
source: musts>pvf1-i flies also showed significantly higher levels of whole animal triacylglycerol (TAG) content than control flies (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TAG assays showing increased TAG/protein ratio, as presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The increase in TAG content from muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown was observed for two independent RNAi lines against pvf1.
source: The increase in total TAG content was observed for two independent RNAi lines against pvf1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using two different RNAi lines (pvf1-i1 and pvf1-i2), as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increase in TAG content of muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies is more pronounced when flies are challenged with a mildly high-sugar diet.
source: The increase in TAG content of musts>pvf1-i flies was more pronounced when flies were challenged with a mildly high-sugar diet (15% w/v added sugar to our standard food) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing TAG content on standard food versus high-sugar diet, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knocking down pvf2 or pvf3 in the adult muscle does not affect total TAG content of the animals.
source: Knocking down either pvf2 or pvf3 in the adult muscle did not affect total TAG content of the animals, further demonstrating that the phenotype is specifically associated with muscle-specific loss of Pvf1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TAG assays comparing pvf1, pvf2, and pvf3 knockdown, as presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies and control flies show comparable incorporation of 14C when fed with 14C-U-Glucose for 24 hrs.
source: When fed with 14C-U-Glucose for 24 hrs, musts>pvf1-i and control flies showed comparable incorporation of 14C in whole fly homogenates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that musts>pvf1-i flies do not eat more than control animals and that the obesity phenotype observed is most likely caused by metabolic defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioactive glucose feeding assays, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The obesity phenotype in muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies is most likely caused by metabolic defects rather than increased food intake.
source: When fed with 14C-U-Glucose for 24 hrs, musts>pvf1-i and control flies showed comparable incorporation of 14C in whole fly homogenates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that musts>pvf1-i flies do not eat more than control animals and that the obesity phenotype observed is most likely caused by metabolic defects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing comparable food intake between experimental and control flies.

claim: Pvf1 protein is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles.
source: Pvf1 is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) where it is stored between the individual myofibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D1', D3') and is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D3,3',3').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining with anti-Pvf1 antibody, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pvf1 protein is stored between individual myofibrils in leg muscles.
source: Pvf1 is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) where it is stored between the individual myofibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D1', D3') and is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D3,3',3').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining showing Pvf1 localization, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pvf1 protein is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs in leg muscles.
source: Pvf1 is abundantly present in the striated tubular leg muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) where it is stored between the individual myofibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D1', D3') and is more concentrated at both the M and Z discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D3,3',3').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining showing Pvf1 localization, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of pvf1 leads to a strong reduction in Pvf1 protein level in leg muscles.
source: To verify the specificity of the signal, we immunostained the leg muscles of musts>pvf1-i flies with anti-Pvf1 antibody and observed a strong reduction in Pvf1 protein level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D2',D4,D4').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining comparing control and pvf1 knockdown flies, as presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The indirect flight muscles (IFMs) do not show any staining for Pvf1.
source: Interestingly, the IFMs did not show any staining for Pvf1 indicating that the protein is primarily stored in the striated tubular muscles in the fly.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining of IFMs showing absence of Pvf1 signal.

claim: Pvf1 protein is primarily stored in the striated tubular muscles in the fly.
source: Interestingly, the IFMs did not show any staining for Pvf1 indicating that the protein is primarily stored in the striated tubular muscles in the fly.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunostaining data showing Pvf1 presence in tubular muscles but not in IFMs.

claim: Single-nuclei RNA-sequencing was performed on adult fly abdominal cuticles to understand transcriptomes of metabolically active tissues.
source: We took advantage of this tool to understand the transcriptomes of tissue types residing in the adult abdominal cuticle that harbors several metabolically active tissues such as the fat body, abdominal-muscles, and oenocytes, which are functionally analogous to adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and liver, respectively, in higher vertebrates (Droujinine and Perrimon, 2016; Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental approach and references to established knowledge about tissue functions.

claim: A total of 80 adult fly abdominal cuticles were dissected and dissociated for single-nuclei RNA-sequencing.
source: To delineate the patterns of gene expression in each of these tissues, we dissected and dissociated a total of 80 adult fly abdominal cuticles (along with the attached adipose tissue and oenocytes) and subjected the single nuclei to 10X genomics-based (Zheng et al., 2017) single-nuclei RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Two independent rounds of sequencing were performed on two biological replicates with 40 animals per replicate.
source: Two independent rounds of sequencing were performed on two biological replicates (with 40 animals per replicate) to obtain a median read depth of 8904 reads per nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental design.

claim: The median read depth obtained from snRNA-seq was 8904 reads per nucleus.
source: Two independent rounds of sequencing were performed on two biological replicates (with 40 animals per replicate) to obtain a median read depth of 8904 reads per nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SoupX was used to eliminate potential ambient RNA contamination from the snRNA-seq analysis.
source: Because tissue dissociations for the single nuclei preparations are often associated with the risk of ambient RNA contamination, our quality control pipeline included SoupX (Young and Behjati, 2018) to eliminate potential ambient RNA from our analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the quality control methodology and citation to the SoupX method.

claim: Harmony was used to correct for batch effects in the two replicates of snRNA-seq data.
source: Further, we used Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) that is integrated into Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019) to correct for batch effects in the two replicates to finally retain 15,280 nuclei with a median of 192 genes per nucleus for downstream analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the data analysis methodology and citations to Harmony and Seurat.

claim: After quality control and batch correction, 15,280 nuclei were retained for downstream analysis.
source: Further, we used Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) that is integrated into Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019) to correct for batch effects in the two replicates to finally retain 15,280 nuclei with a median of 192 genes per nucleus for downstream analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the data analysis results.

claim: The median number of genes detected per nucleus after quality control was 192.
source: Further, we used Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) that is integrated into Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019) to correct for batch effects in the two replicates to finally retain 15,280 nuclei with a median of 192 genes per nucleus for downstream analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the data analysis results.

claim: Clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 identified 10 unique clusters.
source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the clustering analysis results presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers.
source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers, as presented in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The adipose tissue cluster was identified based on expression of apolpp marker.
source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers.

claim: The oenocyte cluster was identified based on expression of fasn3 marker.
source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers.

claim: The muscle cluster was identified based on expression of mhc marker.
source: Our clustering analysis at resolution 0.1 (see Materials and methods) identified 10 unique clusters, where three major clusters were assigned to adipose tissue, oenocytes, and muscle based on known markers for each of these tissue types including apolpp, fasn3, and mhc, respectively (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis using known tissue markers.

claim: The snRNA-seq data was validated using GAL4 lines for enriched genes Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko.
source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I.

claim: Pellino (Pli) specifically expresses in adipose tissue.
source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Sallimus (sls) specifically expresses in muscle.
source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Geko specifically expresses in oenocytes.
source: We validated our snRNA-seq data using GAL4 lines for certain top enriched and novel genes such as Pellino (Pli), sallimus (sls), and geko and found that they specifically express in adipose tissue, muscle, and oenocytes, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using GAL4 lines, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Minor clusters (4-10) are believed to be remnant tissues likely pertaining to gut/malpighian tubule based on enrichment of specific genes.
source: With regard to the rest of the minor clusters (4-10), we believe most of them are remnant tissues most likely pertaining to gut/malpighian tubule based on the enrichment of alphaTry, Whe, and Mur18B (Clusters 4–6, respectively; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns in the minor clusters.

claim: Clusters 7-10 are likely to be part of the ejaculatory bulb based on enrichment of male-specific genes.
source: On the other hand, we consider clusters 7–10 likely to be part of the ejaculatory bulb (Eb) as they are enriched in certain male-specific genes such as bond, EbpIII, soti, and Ebp, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-J; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns showing enrichment of male-specific genes.

claim: Increasing the resolution of clustering analysis to 0.4 leads to identification of 15 unique clusters with unique gene expression signatures.
source: Interestingly, increasing the resolution of the clustering analysis to 0.4 leads to the identification of 15 unique clusters with unique gene expression signatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis at higher resolution, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Some of the clusters identified at resolution 0.4 may reflect potential heterogeneity within the adult adipose tissue.
source: Some of these clusters may reflect potential heterogeneity within the adult adipose tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the biological meaning of the additional clusters identified at higher resolution.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis reveals EGFR and PVR RTK signaling pathway is highly enriched in oenocytes.
source: Interestingly, we found that EGFR and PVR RTK signaling pathway is highly enriched in the oenocytes (Figure 2C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis results presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of Egfr is specifically enriched in the adipose tissue.
source: While the expression of Egfr is specifically enriched in the adipose tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-j), we identify the Pvf1 receptor Pvr to be highly enriched in the oenocytes, albeit a mild enrichment seen in the other clusters (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from snRNA-seq analysis, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-j.

claim: Pvr is highly enriched in oenocytes with mild enrichment in other clusters.
source: While the expression of Egfr is specifically enriched in the adipose tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-j), we identify the Pvf1 receptor Pvr to be highly enriched in the oenocytes, albeit a mild enrichment seen in the other clusters (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from snRNA-seq analysis, as presented in Figure 2D.

claim: PvR is present most prominently on the surface of oenocytes followed by adipose tissue cells.
source: Consistent with the prediction from the snRNA-seq analysis, PvR is present most prominently on the surface of the oenocytes followed by the adipose tissue cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2E, which is consistent with the snRNA-seq predictions.

claim: In leg muscles and indirect flight muscles, PvR localizes to the muscle sarcolemma.
source: In the leg muscles and indirect flight muscles, PvR localizes to the muscle sarcolemma (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although the level of the protein on the sarcolemma of the leg muscles is relatively weak (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The level of PvR protein on the sarcolemma of leg muscles is relatively weak.
source: In the leg muscles and indirect flight muscles, PvR localizes to the muscle sarcolemma (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although the level of the protein on the sarcolemma of the leg muscles is relatively weak (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Oenocyte-specific over-expression of pvrDN leads to obesity phenotypes similar to muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies.
source: Impairing PvR signaling in the adult oenocytes, by over-expressing a dominant negative form of the receptor, pvrDN, (oenots>pvrDN) (Brückner et al., 2004) led to obesity phenotypes similar to musts>Pvf1-i flies (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and TAG assays, as presented in Figure 2F and 2G, with citation to the pvrDN construct.

claim: Oenocyte-specific expression of an RNAi against pvr leads to obesity.
source: Similarly, impairing PvR signaling in the oenocyte by expressing an RNAi against pvr (oenots>pvr-i) also leads to obesity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The obesity phenotype from oenocyte-specific pvrDN expression was also observed in female flies.
source: The obesity phenotype was also observed in oenots>pvrDN female flies, indicating that the phenotype is not caused by loss of PvR signaling in the male accessory glands where the PromE-Gal4 driver is also expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Billeter et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from female flies, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, with citation to the PromE-Gal4 driver expression pattern.

claim: The obesity phenotype in oenocyte-specific pvrDN females is not caused by loss of PvR signaling in male accessory glands.
source: The obesity phenotype was also observed in oenots>pvrDN female flies, indicating that the phenotype is not caused by loss of PvR signaling in the male accessory glands where the PromE-Gal4 driver is also expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Billeter et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing the phenotype in females, with citation to the driver expression pattern.

claim: Over-expressing pvrDN in the adult adipose tissue and muscle does not lead to an obesity phenotype.
source: Surprisingly, over-expressing pvrDN in the adult adipose tissue and muscle did not lead to an obesity phenotype indicating that Pvf/PvR signaling is primarily required in the oenocytes to regulate lipid abundance (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TAG assays and BODIPY staining, as presented in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pvf/PvR signaling is primarily required in the oenocytes to regulate lipid abundance.
source: Surprisingly, over-expressing pvrDN in the adult adipose tissue and muscle did not lead to an obesity phenotype indicating that Pvf/PvR signaling is primarily required in the oenocytes to regulate lipid abundance (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing tissue-specific effects of PvR manipulation.

claim: Muscle-derived Pvf1 signals specifically to the oenocytes to regulate lipid content of the adipose tissue and steatosis in the oenocytes.
source: These results suggest that muscle-derived Pvf1 signals specifically to the oenocytes to regulate lipid content of the adipose tissue and steatosis in the oenocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing tissue-specific effects.

claim: Two independent and validated RNAi transgenes against ERK failed to replicate the obesity phenotype observed in oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies.
source: Two independent and validated RNAi transgenes against ERK failed to replicate the obesity phenotype observed in oenots>pvrDN flies, suggesting that PvR signaling in the oenocytes regulates lipid levels via an ERK-independent mechanism (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements using two ERK RNAi lines, as presented in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: PvR signaling in the oenocytes regulates lipid levels via an ERK-independent mechanism.
source: Two independent and validated RNAi transgenes against ERK failed to replicate the obesity phenotype observed in oenots>pvrDN flies, suggesting that PvR signaling in the oenocytes regulates lipid levels via an ERK-independent mechanism (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing no effect of ERK knockdown on lipid accumulation.

claim: Previous studies in Drosophila S2 and Kc cells have shown that PvR can activate the TOR pathway.
source: Previous studies in Drosophila S2 and Kc cells have shown that PvR can also activate the TOR pathway (Sopko et al., 2015; Tran et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in cell culture systems.

claim: Oenocyte-specific over-expression of tsc1 and tsc2 leads to massive accumulation of neutral lipids in both adipose tissue and oenocytes.
source: Similar to musts>pvf1-i and oenots>pvrDN flies, oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies showed massive accumulation of neutral lipids in both the adipose tissue and the oenocytes (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Oenocyte-specific knockdown of Pi3K92E leads to steatosis phenotypes.
source: Oenocyte-specific loss of either Pi3K92E and the regulatory subunit Pi3K21B led to steatosis phenotypes (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Oenocyte-specific knockdown of Pi3K21B leads to steatosis phenotypes.
source: Oenocyte-specific loss of either Pi3K92E and the regulatory subunit Pi3K21B led to steatosis phenotypes (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Oenocyte-specific loss of akt1 leads to steatosis phenotypes.
source: Additionally, oenocyte-specific loss of akt1 also led to steatosis phenotypes indicating that the Pi3K-Akt1 pathway in the oenocytes regulates lipid homeostasis (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The Pi3K-Akt1 pathway in the oenocytes regulates lipid homeostasis.
source: Additionally, oenocyte-specific loss of akt1 also led to steatosis phenotypes indicating that the Pi3K-Akt1 pathway in the oenocytes regulates lipid homeostasis (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of Pi3K and Akt1 manipulation on lipid accumulation.

claim: Pi3K/Akt1/TOR signaling in the oenocyte protects against obesity.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that Pi3K/Akt1/TOR signaling in the oenocyte protects against obesity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing effects of pathway components on obesity.

claim: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies show a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in oenocytes compared to controls.
source: Both musts>pvf1-i flies and oenots>pvrDN flies showed a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in the oenocytes compared to Gal4 alone controls (Figure 4A, B, C), indicating that muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from p4EBP immunostaining, as presented in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claim: Oenocyte-specific pvrDN over-expression flies show a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in oenocytes compared to controls.
source: Both musts>pvf1-i flies and oenots>pvrDN flies showed a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in the oenocytes compared to Gal4 alone controls (Figure 4A, B, C), indicating that muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from p4EBP immunostaining, as presented in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claim: Muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
source: Both musts>pvf1-i flies and oenots>pvrDN flies showed a strong and significant down-regulation of p4EBP signal in the oenocytes compared to Gal4 alone controls (Figure 4A, B, C), indicating that muscle Pvf regulates TORC1 signaling in the oenocyte.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing reduced p4EBP levels (a TOR target) upon Pvf/PvR pathway disruption.

claim: The extent of p4EBP down-regulation in muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown and oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies is similar to oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 over-expression flies.
source: Consistently, the extent of p4EBP down-regulation is similar to what is observed in oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies that were used as a positive control for the assay (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing p4EBP levels across different genotypes, as presented in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Oenocyte-specific loss of insulin receptor signaling does not affect p4EBP levels.
source: Interestingly, oenocyte-specific loss of insulin receptor signaling (oenots>inrDN) failed to affect p4EBP levels (Figure 4B , C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from p4EBP immunostaining, as presented in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Oenocyte-specific tsc2 knockdown strongly suppresses the obesity phenotype induced by oenocyte-specific pvrDN expression.
source: tsc2 knockdown strongly suppressed the obesity phenotype induced by oenocyte-specific expression of pvrDN (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Oenocyte-specific co-expression of constitutively active rheb (rhebAV4) completely rescues the obesity phenotype observed in oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies.
source: Oenocyte-specific co-expression of rhebAV4 completely rescued the obesity phenotype observed in oenots>pvrDN flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: TOR signaling functions downstream of PvR in the oenocyte to negatively regulate lipid deposits.
source: Altogether, these observations suggest that TOR signaling functions downstream of PvR in the oenocyte to negatively regulate lipid deposits.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including p4EBP measurements and genetic rescue experiments.

claim: In Drosophila, insulin/Pi3K/Akt signaling can activate the TOR pathway, similar to vertebrates.
source: Similar to vertebrates, the Drosophila TOR pathway can be activated by insulin/Pi3K/Akt signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about TOR pathway regulation in Drosophila and vertebrates.

claim: Oenocyte-specific over-expression of inrDN does not show any increase in lipid accumulation in adipose tissue or oenocytes compared to control flies.
source: oenots>inrDN flies did not show any increase in accumulation of lipids either in the adipose tissue or the oenocytes compared to control flies (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Oenocyte-specific co-expression of inrDN and pvrDN results in flies that are still obese with excessive lipid accumulation in adipose tissue but suppressed lipid accumulation in oenocytes.
source: Strikingly, while oenots>pvrDN; inrDN flies were still obese and showed excessive accumulation of lipids in the adipose tissue, lipid accumulation in oenocytes was suppressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Right most panels, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating that InR signaling is required for lipid accumulation in the oenocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: InR signaling is required for lipid accumulation in the oenocytes.
source: Strikingly, while oenots>pvrDN; inrDN flies were still obese and showed excessive accumulation of lipids in the adipose tissue, lipid accumulation in oenocytes was suppressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Right most panels, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), indicating that InR signaling is required for lipid accumulation in the oenocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing differential effects of InR and PvR signaling on oenocyte versus adipose tissue lipid accumulation.

claim: A previous report showed that activation of InR signaling in oenocytes led to accumulation of lipids both under fed and starved conditions.
source: Interestingly, a previous report showed that activation of InR signaling in oenocytes led to accumulation of lipids both under fed and starved conditions (Chatterjee et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Oenocyte-specific activation of TOR (by tsc2 knockdown) does not lead to lipid accumulation in oenocytes or adipose tissue.
source: To further characterize the oenocyte-specific role of TOR on lipid accumulation, we activated TOR in the oenocytes (oenots>tsc2-i) and did not detect lipid accumulation either in the oenocytes or the adipose tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and lipid droplet size measurements, as presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: In Drosophila, muscle-derived Pvf1 signals through PvR in the oenocyte to activate TOR, which protects the animal against obesity.
source: Altogether, we demonstrate that in Drosophila, muscle-derived Pvf1 signals through PvR in the oenocyte to activate TOR, which in turn protects the animal against obesity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing the complete signaling pathway.

claim: Drosophila oenocytes are known to facilitate starvation-induced lipid mobilization in larvae.
source: Drosophila oenocytes are known to facilitate starvation-induced lipid mobilization in the Drosophila larvae and loss of this tissue leads to increased starvation sensitivity (Gutierrez et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss of oenocytes in Drosophila larvae leads to increased starvation sensitivity.
source: Drosophila oenocytes are known to facilitate starvation-induced lipid mobilization in the Drosophila larvae and loss of this tissue leads to increased starvation sensitivity (Gutierrez et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In adult flies, oenocytes play a role in imparting starvation resistance by regulating production of very long chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) for waterproofing of the cuticle.
source: Similarly, in adult flies the oenocytes play a role in imparting starvation resistance by regulating production of very long chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) for waterproofing of the cuticle, especially when flies are starved under lower humidity conditions, and possibly by regulating lipid mobilization (Chatterjee et al., 2014; Storelli et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies show increased starvation resistance compared to control flies.
source: Compared to control flies, musts>pvf1-i and oenots>pvrDN animals showed increased starvation resistance, suggesting that they are capable of mobilizing stored nutrients in response to starvation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from starvation resistance assays, as presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Oenocyte-specific pvrDN over-expression flies show increased starvation resistance compared to control flies.
source: Compared to control flies, musts>pvf1-i and oenots>pvrDN animals showed increased starvation resistance, suggesting that they are capable of mobilizing stored nutrients in response to starvation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from starvation resistance assays, as presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The increased starvation resistance of muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown and oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies is capable of mobilizing stored nutrients in response to starvation.
source: Compared to control flies, musts>pvf1-i and oenots>pvrDN animals showed increased starvation resistance, suggesting that they are capable of mobilizing stored nutrients in response to starvation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from starvation resistance data.

claim: The improved starvation resistance of muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown and oenocyte-specific pvrDN flies most likely reflects higher levels of stored TAGs that can be used for longer duration.
source: The improved starvation resistance of musts>pvf1-i and oenots>pvrDN flies most likely reflects the fact that these animals had higher levels of stored TAGs and hence were able to use these reserves for a longer duration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from starvation resistance data combined with previous TAG measurements.

claim: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies show similar rates of lipid mobilization from TAG stores compared to control flies.
source: Interestingly, musts>pvf1-i flies showed similar rates of lipid mobilization from TAG stores compared to control flies (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioisotope chase assays, as presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 over-expression flies show comparable rates of lipid mobilization compared to control animals.
source: Similarly, oenots>tsc1, tsc2 and oenots>pvrDN flies also showed comparable rates of lipid mobilization compared to control animals, indicating that loss of the muscle-to-oenocyte Pvf1 signaling axis does not impair lipid mobilization (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioisotope chase assays, as presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Oenocyte-specific pvrDN over-expression flies show comparable rates of lipid mobilization compared to control animals.
source: Similarly, oenots>tsc1, tsc2 and oenots>pvrDN flies also showed comparable rates of lipid mobilization compared to control animals, indicating that loss of the muscle-to-oenocyte Pvf1 signaling axis does not impair lipid mobilization (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioisotope chase assays, as presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of the muscle-to-oenocyte Pvf1 signaling axis does not impair lipid mobilization.
source: Similarly, oenots>tsc1, tsc2 and oenots>pvrDN flies also showed comparable rates of lipid mobilization compared to control animals, indicating that loss of the muscle-to-oenocyte Pvf1 signaling axis does not impair lipid mobilization (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing no difference in lipid mobilization rates.

claim: Muscle-specific pvf1 knockdown flies show an increased rate of 14C incorporation into TAG fractions compared to control animals.
source: We found that musts>pvf1-i, oenots>tsc1, tsc2, and oenots>pvrDN flies all showed an increased rate of 14C incorporation into TAG fractions compared to control animals (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioisotope incorporation assays, as presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 over-expression flies show an increased rate of 14C incorporation into TAG fractions compared to control animals.
source: We found that musts>pvf1-i, oenots>tsc1, tsc2, and oenots>pvrDN flies all showed an increased rate of 14C incorporation into TAG fractions compared to control animals (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioisotope incorporation assays, as presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Oenocyte-specific pvrDN over-expression flies show an increased rate of 14C incorporation into TAG fractions compared to control animals.
source: We found that musts>pvf1-i, oenots>tsc1, tsc2, and oenots>pvrDN flies all showed an increased rate of 14C incorporation into TAG fractions compared to control animals (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioisotope incorporation assays, as presented in Figure 5E.

claim: In absence of effects on lipid mobilization, the increased rate of lipid incorporation indicates an increased rate of lipid synthesis in the experimental flies.
source: In absence of any effects on lipid mobilization, the increased rate of lipid incorporation indicates an increased rate of lipid synthesis in the experimental flies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing increased incorporation without changes in mobilization.

claim: Expression levels of fasn2 and fasn3 are strongly downregulated in oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 over-expression flies.
source: While expression levels of acc and fasn1 did not change in oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies, expression levels of fasn2 and fasn3 were strongly downregulated (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR, as presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Expression levels of acc and fasn1 do not change in oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 over-expression flies.
source: While expression levels of acc and fasn1 did not change in oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies, expression levels of fasn2 and fasn3 were strongly downregulated (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR, as presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Loss of TOR signaling downregulates lipogenic genes in the oenocytes.
source: This indicates that loss of TOR signaling downregulates lipogenic genes in the oenocytes, and that the increased lipid synthesis observed in oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies is caused by a mechanism independent of the role of TOR in regulating the expression of lipogenic genes in the oenocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from RT-qPCR data showing reduced expression of oenocyte-specific lipogenic genes.

claim: The increased lipid synthesis observed in oenocyte-specific tsc1,tsc2 over-expression flies is caused by a mechanism independent of TOR's role in regulating expression of lipogenic genes in oenocytes.
source: This indicates that loss of TOR signaling downregulates lipogenic genes in the oenocytes, and that the increased lipid synthesis observed in oenots>tsc1,tsc2 flies is caused by a mechanism independent of the role of TOR in regulating the expression of lipogenic genes in the oenocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the paradoxical observation of increased lipid synthesis despite reduced lipogenic gene expression.

claim: When adult flies emerge from their pupal cases, the adult adipose tissue has very low stored lipid content.
source: When adult flies emerge from their pupal cases the adult adipose tissue has very low stored lipid content (Storelli et al., 2019), and adipose tissue cells of post-eclosion flies are also notably small in size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, left most panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study and experimental data from imaging, as presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adipose tissue cells of post-eclosion flies are notably small in size.
source: When adult flies emerge from their pupal cases the adult adipose tissue has very low stored lipid content (Storelli et al., 2019), and adipose tissue cells of post-eclosion flies are also notably small in size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, left most panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging, as presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over the course of 3 to 7 days post-eclosion, the adipose tissue builds up its lipid stores through feeding and de novo lipid synthesis.
source: Over the course of the next 3 to 7 days the adipose tissue builds up its lipid stores through feeding and de novo lipid synthesis and expands significantly in size both at cellular and tissue levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, middle and right most panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging showing adipose tissue expansion, as presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The adipose tissue expands significantly in size both at cellular and tissue levels during the 3 to 7 days post-eclosion.
source: Over the course of the next 3 to 7 days the adipose tissue builds up its lipid stores through feeding and de novo lipid synthesis and expands significantly in size both at cellular and tissue levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, middle and right most panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging, as presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average size of lipid droplets does not change drastically during the adipose tissue lipid build-up period.
source: While the average size of the lipid droplets does not change drastically during this period, the number of lipid droplets per cell increases drastically and a large number of smaller lipid droplets start appearing in the adipose tissue cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging, as presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of lipid droplets per cell increases drastically during the adipose tissue lipid build-up period.
source: While the average size of the lipid droplets does not change drastically during this period, the number of lipid droplets per cell increases drastically and a large number of smaller lipid droplets start appearing in the adipose tissue cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging, as presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A large number of smaller lipid droplets start appearing in adipose tissue cells during the lipid build-up period.
source: While the average size of the lipid droplets does not change drastically during this period, the number of lipid droplets per cell increases drastically and a large number of smaller lipid droplets start appearing in the adipose tissue cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging, as presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Build up of adipose tissue lipid stores happens by formation of new lipid droplets that become bigger in size as adipose tissue lipid build up progresses.
source: These observations suggest that build up of adipose tissue lipid stores happens by formation of new lipid droplets that become bigger in size as adipose tissue lipid build up progresses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from imaging data showing changes in lipid droplet number and size over time.

claim: Muscle-specific expression levels of pvf1 is low in newly eclosed flies and increases rapidly over the course of the next 7 days.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we find that muscle-specific expression levels of pvf1 is low in newly eclosed flies and increases rapidly over the course of the next 7 days (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR, as presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Muscle-specific over-expression of pvf1 from day 1 of eclosion leads to accumulation of much lower number of large lipid droplets per adipose tissue cell compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, musts>pvf1 flies tend to accumulate much lower number of large lipid droplets per adipose tissue cell (Figure 6B, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and quantification, as presented in Figure 6B and 6D.

claim: Muscle-specific over-expression of pvf1 from day 1 of eclosion leads to larger number of empty adipose tissue cells per animal compared to control flies.
source: Additionally, the experimental animals tend to have larger number of empty adipose tissue cells per animal compared to control flies (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BODIPY staining and quantification, as presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Muscle-derived Pvf1 helps terminate the adipose tissue lipid build up phase by suppressing lipid synthesis by signaling to the Drosophila oenocytes.
source: These results suggest that muscle-derived Pvf1 helps terminate the adipose tissue lipid build up phase by suppressing lipid synthesis by signaling to the Drosophila oenocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of pvf1 over-expression on adipose tissue lipid accumulation during the build-up phase.

claim: Muscle-Pvf1 serves as an inhibitory signal for suppressing de-novo lipid synthesis once the adult adipose tissue has accumulated sufficient lipid stores at the end of the adipose tissue lipid build-up phase.
source: Taken together our study indicates that muscle-Pvf1 serves as an inhibitory signal for suppressing de-novo lipid synthesis once the adult adipose tissue has accumulated sufficient lipid stores at the end of the adipose tissue lipid build-up phase.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing the temporal pattern of pvf1 expression and its effects on lipid accumulation.

claim: The snRNA-seq data of the adult abdominal region will serve as an invaluable resource to further understand the biology of adipose tissue, oenocytes, and abdominal muscles.
source: Our snRNA-seq data of the adult abdominal region that includes adipose tissue, oenocytes, and abdominal muscles will also serve as an invaluable resource to further understand the biology of these organs.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the future utility of the generated dataset.

claim: A searchable webtool was created to facilitate visualization and exploration of the snRNA-seq gene expression profiles.
source: To facilitate visualization of this rich resource of gene expression profiles, we have created a searchable webtool where users can mine and explore the data (https://www.flyrnai.org/scRNA/abdomen/).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the created resource.

claim: The PDGF/VEGF family of signaling ligands have co-evolved with multicellularity.
source: The PDGF/VEGF family of signaling ligands have co-evolved with multicellularity and are proposed to signal in the context of organisms with tissue-level organization (Holmes and Zachary, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: PDGF/VEGF ligands are proposed to signal in the context of organisms with tissue-level organization.
source: The PDGF/VEGF family of signaling ligands have co-evolved with multicellularity and are proposed to signal in the context of organisms with tissue-level organization (Holmes and Zachary, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: VEGF family ligands, including VEGF-A and VEGF-B, influence metabolic responses such as adiposity, insulin resistance and browning of fat.
source: VEGF family ligands, including VEGF-A and VEGF-B, influence metabolic responses such as adiposity, insulin resistance and browning of fat (Elias et al., 2012; Hagberg et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2012; Robciuc et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2012; Sung et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Mechanisms by which VEGF ligands regulate lipid metabolism are complex and multiple context dependent and confounding models of their action have been proposed.
source: However, mechanisms by which these molecules regulate lipid metabolism are complex and multiple context dependent and confounding models of their action have been proposed (Elias et al., 2012; Hagberg et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2012; Robciuc et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2012; Sung et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies showing varied results.

claim: In previous studies, the effect of VEGFs on obesity and insulin resistance have been attributed to their roles in modulating tissue micro-vascularization and endothelial cell biology.
source: Nevertheless, in all these studies the effect of VEGFs on obesity and insulin resistance have been attributed to their roles in modulating tissue micro-vascularization and endothelial cell biology.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from citations to previous studies.

claim: PDGF signaling ligands PDGF-BB and -CC have been implicated in adipose tissue expansion, glucose metabolism, and thermogenesis in beige fat by influencing remodeling of tissue vascularization.
source: Similarly, PDGF signaling ligands PDGF-BB and -CC have also been implicated in adipose tissue expansion, glucose metabolism, and thermogenesis in beige fat, by influencing remodeling of tissue vascularization (Onogi et al., 2017; Seki et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Signaling to non-endothelial cell types by PDGF/VEGF ligands could play equally important roles in regulating obesity and insulin resistance.
source: Nevertheless, signaling to non-endothelial cell types by PDGF/VEGF ligands could play equally important roles in regulating obesity and insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about alternative mechanisms of PDGF/VEGF action.

claim: In Drosophila, the PDGF/VEGF pathway ligands are encoded by three genes: pvf1, pvf2, and pvf3.
source: In Drosophila, the PDGF/VEGF pathway ligands are encoded by three genes, pvf1, pvf2, and pvf3 (Cho et al., 2002; Duchek et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila PDGF/VEGF ligands signal through a receptor-tyrosine kinase (RTK) encoded by pvr.
source: Similar to vertebrate PDGFs/VEGFs, these molecules signal through a receptor-tyrosine Kkinase (RTK) encoded by pvr.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the Drosophila PDGF/VEGF signaling pathway.

claim: Once bound to the receptor, Pvfs are known to primarily activate the Ras/Raf/ERK intracellular cascade.
source: Once bound to the receptor, Pvfs are known to primarily activate the Ras/Raf/ERK intracellular cascade (Duchek et al., 2001; Heino et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis shows that Pvf1 is closely related to both VEGFs and PDGFs and most likely plays the dual role of representing both these divergent signaling pathways in the fly.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the Pvfs show that Pvf1 is closely related to both VEGFs and PDGFs and most likely plays the dual role of representing both these divergent signaling pathways in the fly (Holmes and Zachary, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Pvf2 and Pvf3 are more ancestral forms of the protein and are phylogenetically distinct.
source: Pvf2 and Pvf3 are more ancestral forms of the protein and are phylogenetically distinct with Pvf2 lacking the conserved cysteine necessary for forming the cysteine knot structure characteristic of this family of ligands (Holmes and Zachary, 2005; Kasap, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pvf2 lacks the conserved cysteine necessary for forming the cysteine knot structure characteristic of PDGF/VEGF family ligands.
source: Pvf2 and Pvf3 are more ancestral forms of the protein and are phylogenetically distinct with Pvf2 lacking the conserved cysteine necessary for forming the cysteine knot structure characteristic of this family of ligands (Holmes and Zachary, 2005; Kasap, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Core metabolic organs and signaling mechanisms that regulate metabolic homeostasis are highly conserved between Drosophila and vertebrates.
source: Core metabolic organs and signaling mechanisms that regulate metabolic homeostasis are also highly conserved between Drosophila and vertebrates (Droujinine and Perrimon, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous review.

claim: Metabolic organ systems that are functionally and structurally analogous to the vertebrate adipose tissue, muscle, intestine, and liver exist in Drosophila.
source: Metabolic organ systems that are functionally and structurally analogous to the vertebrate adipose tissue, muscle, intestine, and liver exist in Drosophila (Gutierrez et al., 2007; Leopold and Perrimon, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Drosophila adipose tissue (fat body) functions as the primary site for lipid storage.
source: The Drosophila adipose tissue (also called the fat body) functions as the primary site for lipid storage.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila metabolism.

claim: The Drosophila adipose tissue is the key site for sensing the nutrient status of the animal and coupling it to systemic growth, metabolism, and feeding behavior.
source: The adipose tissue is also the key site for sensing the nutrient status of the animal and coupling it to systemic growth, metabolism, and feeding behavior (Colombani et al., 2003; Grönke et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The roles of the liver are shared between the adipose tissue and specialized hepatocyte-like cells called the oenocytes in Drosophila.
source: The roles of the liver are shared between the adipose tissue and specialized hepatocyte-like cells called the oenocytes, with the adipose tissue being the primary site of glycogen storage and the oenocytes playing the roles of lipid mobilization and synthesis of specialized lipid molecules (Gutierrez et al., 2007; Makki et al., 2014; Storelli et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Drosophila adipose tissue is the primary site of glycogen storage.
source: The roles of the liver are shared between the adipose tissue and specialized hepatocyte-like cells called the oenocytes, with the adipose tissue being the primary site of glycogen storage and the oenocytes playing the roles of lipid mobilization and synthesis of specialized lipid molecules (Gutierrez et al., 2007; Makki et al., 2014; Storelli et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila oenocytes play roles in lipid mobilization and synthesis of specialized lipid molecules.
source: The roles of the liver are shared between the adipose tissue and specialized hepatocyte-like cells called the oenocytes, with the adipose tissue being the primary site of glycogen storage and the oenocytes playing the roles of lipid mobilization and synthesis of specialized lipid molecules (Gutierrez et al., 2007; Makki et al., 2014; Storelli et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A number of hormonal signals emanating from the Drosophila adipose tissue, gut, and muscle have been characterized and shown to play diverse roles.
source: A number of hormonal signals emanating from the Drosophila adipose tissue, gut, and muscle have been characterized and shown to play roles as diverse as regulation of insulin and glucagon (AKH in Drosophila) release, nutrient uptake in the gut, and mitochondrial metabolism (Chng et al., 2014; Droujinine and Perrimon, 2016; Ghosh and O'Connor, 2014; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Components of core metabolic pathways such as the TOR signaling pathway are highly conserved in the fly.
source: Components of core metabolic pathways such as the TOR signaling pathway are also highly conserved in the fly and much has been learned about the fundamental principles of the regulation of TOR and its roles in growth and aging from studies in Drosophila (Antikainen et al., 2017; Colombani et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2008; Piper and Partridge, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Much has been learned about the fundamental principles of TOR regulation and its roles in growth and aging from studies in Drosophila.
source: Components of core metabolic pathways such as the TOR signaling pathway are also highly conserved in the fly and much has been learned about the fundamental principles of the regulation of TOR and its roles in growth and aging from studies in Drosophila (Antikainen et al., 2017; Colombani et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2008; Piper and Partridge, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila Pvfs have been primarily studied in the context of their roles in embryonic development, cell motility, and specification of immune cells.
source: Drosophila Pvfs have been primarily studied in the context of their roles in embryonic development, cell motility, and specification of immune cells (Duchek et al., 2001; Ishimaru et al., 2004; Rosin et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The role of Drosophila Pvfs in metabolism remains less explored.
source: However, the role of these signaling peptides in metabolism remains less explored.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature showing limited studies on Pvf metabolic roles.

claim: This study identifies Drosophila PDGF/VEGF ortholog Pvf1 as a tubular muscle derived signaling factor (myokine) that regulates systemic lipid stores by inhibiting lipid synthesis.
source: Here, we identify the Drosophila PDGF/VEGF ortholog, Pvf1, as a tubular muscle derived signaling factor (myokine) that regulates systemic lipid stores by inhibiting lipid synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Single-nuclei RNA sequencing identifies adult oenocytes as one of the primary targets of Pvf signaling.
source: Additionally, by subjecting the metabolically active organ systems that reside in Drosophila abdomen (muscle, oenocytes, and adipose tissue) to single-nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNA-Seq), we identify the adult oenocytes to be one of the primary targets of Pvf signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from snRNA-seq data showing enrichment of PvR in oenocytes.

claim: Muscle-derived Pvf1 signals to the oenocytes where it activates the PvR/Pi3K/Akt1/TOR signaling pathway that inhibits lipid synthesis.
source: We provide further evidence that muscle-derived Pvf1 signals to the oenocytes where it activates the PvR/Pi3K/Akt1/TOR signaling pathway that in turn inhibits lipid synthesis in the organism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing the complete signaling pathway.

claim: Muscle-derived pvf1 plays an important role in regulating the build up of adult adipose tissue lipid stores in newly eclosed flies.
source: We also find that muscle-derived pvf1 plays an important role in regulating the build up of adult adipose tissue lipid stores in newly eclosed flies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing temporal expression of pvf1 and effects of its manipulation.

claim: Flies eclose from their pupal case with limited adult adipose tissue lipid stores.
source: Flies eclose from their pupal case with limited adult adipose tissue lipid stores.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging and citation to previous work.

claim: Post eclosion, flies enter a developmental stage marked by increased lipid synthesis needed for accumulation of adipose tissue lipid stores.
source: Post eclosion they enter a developmental stage that is marked by increased lipid synthesis needed for accumulation of the adipose tissue lipid stores.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing lipid accumulation over time post-eclosion.

claim: pvf1 expression in the muscle increases rapidly during the adipose tissue lipid build-up stage.
source: pvf1 expression in the muscle increases rapidly during this stage and premature expression of pvf1 in the muscle interferes with the process of lipid accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR showing temporal expression pattern.

claim: Premature expression of pvf1 in the muscle interferes with the process of lipid accumulation.
source: pvf1 expression in the muscle increases rapidly during this stage and premature expression of pvf1 in the muscle interferes with the process of lipid accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pvf1 over-expression experiments.

claim: Muscle-Pvf1 serves as an inhibitory signal for suppressing de-novo lipid synthesis once the adult adipose tissue has accumulated sufficient lipid stores at the end of the adipose tissue lipid build-up phase.
source: Taken together our study indicates that muscle-Pvf1 serves as an inhibitory signal for suppressing de-novo lipid synthesis once the adult adipose tissue has accumulated sufficient lipid stores at the end of the adipose tissue lipid build-up phase.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing temporal regulation and functional effects.

claim: This is the first evidence in a metazoan of a PDGF/VEGF ligand acting as a myokine that regulates systemic lipid homeostasis by activating TOR in hepatocyte-like cells.
source: Our findings provide the first evidence in a metazoan of a PDGF/VEGF ligand acting as a myokine that regulates systemic lipid homeostasis by activating TOR in hepatocyte-like cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the novelty of the findings in the context of existing literature.
